findings.rationale: Claim: FsResolver::read joins the component path taken verbatim from a compose `use ... from` clause onto its base with no containment check (no canonicalisation, no base-prefix assertion), so a spec containing `../../..` segments or an absolute path reads any file the process can read; PathBuf::join with an absolute path discards the base entirely. component_error (compose.rs:165-207) then embeds the inner parse/lower message into the surfaced diagnostic, which is a plausible content-disclosure channel. Evidence status: unverified static reading only — I have no execution environment, did not run any test, and fsl_syntax (which produces `path`) is not in my context, so I could not confirm that the parser does not already reject traversal segments. Exposure is conditional on untrusted specs reaching this resolver; the CLI usage shown is local. Requested evidence: a reproduction test resolving a `use` with `../` and with an absolute path, and confirmation of whether fsl-core backs the Worker envelope referenced in diagnostics.rs:12-27.

Claim: rewrite_compose_statements is infallible and discharges resolve_alias_statement's Result with .expect("compose alias validation occurs during lowering"), but that Err is reachable from user input: resolve_alias_statement -> resolve_alias_binder (line 999) -> resolve_alias_qualified_name returns Err for an unknown alias namespace (lines 1138-1147). No prior validation pass over compose `common init` statements exists in lower_compose — components are loaded, then compose items are walked (lines 335-359) and this is the only compose branch that panics instead of returning CoreError, unlike the sibling branches at 351-356 which use `?`. Effect: an unknown alias in a typed binder inside `common init` aborts the process instead of producing a diagnostic. The same Err path also loses position (line/column hardcoded to 1:1 at 1142-1143), contradicting the file's own anchoring rationale at 155-164. Evidence status: unverified — reachability depends on the compose grammar admitting `forall x: alias.T` inside `common init`, which I could not check because fsl_syntax is not in my context; the `?`/Result plumbing at 999 implies it is admitted. Requested evidence: a fixture compose document with an unknown-alias binder in `common init` asserting a CoreError rather than a panic.

Claim: in resolve_alias_statement the assignment target is passed through unchanged (line 973) while the right-hand side is alias-resolved, so `alias.field := expr` in a compose `common init` keeps an LValue::Field(Var(alias), field) that no later stage rewrites to the prefixed `alias__field` name. The component-side counterpart rewrite_statement does rewrite its lvalue (line 655), so the two statement rewriters disagree on whether targets carry names. Consequence is either a dangling target name downstream or, if a common state field happens to share the alias's name, a silent write to the wrong variable. Evidence status: unverified — I did not confirm the compose grammar admits alias-qualified assignment targets, and the downstream kernel name resolver is not in my context, so I cannot say whether the failure is a clear error or silent. Requested evidence: a compose fixture assigning to `alias.field` in `common init` plus the lowered kernel AST for that case.

Claim: rewrite_component_item's terminal arm returns SpecItem::Until, Unless, Def, VerifyBounds, Entity and Number completely unmodified, while every other name-introducing item is alias-prefixed and every embedded expression is state/const-rewritten. Merged component items are pushed into the shared static_items list (line 330), so two components each declaring `until P` or `def f(..)` produce duplicate top-level names in the composed spec, and the bodies of those items still reference the component's original, now-renamed state and const names. Supporting fact from the same file: ComponentNames::collect deliberately records Until/Unless names into `properties` (lines 143-146) and action names into `actions`, yet neither set is ever read anywhere in this module — the fields are dead, which is consistent with an intended handling step that was not written. Evidence status: unverified — I ran nothing; whether the mismatch surfaces as a downstream name-resolution error or as a silent capture depends on the kernel name resolver, which is not in my context. Requested evidence: a compose fixture with two components each declaring an `until`/`unless` property (and one with a `def`) and the resulting kernel AST.

Claim: SpecItem::Enum is rewritten by prefixing the type name only; `members` is moved through untouched, and enum member names are not tracked by ComponentNames at all, so rewrite_expr never renames a bare Expr::Var referring to a member. Cross-file support that members inhabit a flat value namespace rather than being qualified by their type: db.rs builds enum members as plain strings (307-312) and then references them as Expr::Var(member) via indexed() (86-91). Consequently two composed components whose enums share a member spelling merge into one namespace with a duplicated member, and every member reference in either component becomes ambiguous. Evidence status: unverified — no execution or type check; the conclusion that duplicate members are actually harmful rests on the db.rs usage pattern above and on the absence of any member-qualification code in this module, not on a run of the kernel resolver. Requested evidence: a compose fixture with two components declaring enums that share a member name, plus the resolver's behaviour on the composed spec.

Claim: rewrite_action_items rewrites every item against one immutable `bound` set built solely from the action's parameters (compose.rs:463-468); ActionItem::Let (623-625) keeps its binder name but never adds it to `bound`, so if a `let` name coincides with one of the component's state fields or consts, all later references to the let-bound name satisfy the guard at 711-714 and are silently rewritten to `alias__name`, rebinding them from the local let to the component's state variable. This is inconsistent with the same module's deliberate scope tracking for quantifier, aggregate and forall binders (796-798, 810-812, 675-677), which is why I read it as an omission rather than an intended rule. Evidence status: unverified — I have no compiler or test run; the defect is only reachable if the language permits a `let` name that shadows a state/const name, which I could not check since fsl_syntax and any well-formedness checker are outside my context. Requested evidence: a component action with `let x = ...` where `x` is also a state field, composed under an alias, and the lowered body.

Claim: column identity in the generated catalog is the string `col_{safe(table)}_{safe(column)}` (37-39), and `safe` is not injective — it maps every non-alphanumeric character to '_' — while the joining separator is itself '_'. Distinct declared columns therefore collide: (table "a_b", column "c") and (table "a", column "b_c") both yield `col_a_b_c`, as do (table "a-b", column "c") and (table "a_b", column "c"). The colliding member is emitted into the Column enum built by mapping over the BTreeMap keys (309), so the enum gets a duplicate member and the column_exists/column_backfilled/column_not_null maps conflate two different columns' migration effects and compatibility invariants — a silently wrong verification result rather than an error. invariant_name (45-54) applies the same non-injective `safe` per part, so generated invariant names inherit the collision even though its separator was chosen carefully. Evidence status: unverified — reasoning over the string construction only; I ran no test and cannot confirm from the given files whether an earlier stage rejects table/column names containing non-alphanumeric characters or embedded underscores. Requested evidence: a db fixture declaring `a_b.c` and `a.b_c` and an assertion that the two columns remain distinct in the lowered catalog.

Claim: the "rename" lowering clears the source column first — `column_exists`, `column_backfilled` and `column_not_null` for `member` are all assigned false at 479-481 — and only afterwards assigns the target's nullability from `indexed("column_not_null", &member)` at 494-499, i.e. it reads the value it has just overwritten. Under sequential statement semantics the target's not_null is therefore always false and a rename silently drops a NOT NULL constraint, which the read of the source value shows was not the intent; the neighbouring "split" arm assigns the literal false at 524-529 when it means false. Internal support for sequential semantics: the "backfill" and "set_not_null" arms (439-465) emit `requires column_exists[m]` / `requires column_backfilled[m]` that can only be satisfiable after an "add"/"backfill" op earlier in the same migration if earlier assignments are visible to later items. Evidence status: unverified and conditional — I have no execution environment and the kernel statement semantics (sequential vs. simultaneous/pre-state assignment) are decided outside the files I was given, so if assignments are simultaneous this claim is wrong. Requested evidence: the kernel lowering's assignment-ordering rule, or a model-check of a migration that renames a not_null column and asserts the target ends not_null.

Claim: the artifact-compatibility loop iterates the columns named by an artifact's read/write capabilities (730) and emits an invariant over `column_member(column)` (789) without requiring that column to be declared in the database catalog. The code itself treats non-membership as possible — `if let Some(column_decl) = columns.get(column)` at 750 guards only the secondary origin site — so an artifact referencing a mistyped or removed column produces an invariant over an identifier that is not a member of the Column enum built at 307-312, and no diagnostic is produced here (contrast the artifact lookup at 699-701, which skips silently rather than reporting). Evidence status: unverified — static reading only; whether the dangling member surfaces as a kernel type error, a spurious verification failure, or an accidental match against another name depends on the resolver, which is not in my context, and an earlier validation of artifact capability columns may exist in code I was not given. Requested evidence: a db fixture whose artifact reads an undeclared column, and the resulting diagnostic or lowered spec.
